ED-216 [UI] One dialog seam for every SwiftUI `.alert`, `.confirmationDialog` and NSAlert (TimelineRows STOP 2). SOURCE FACT: six
sites in 1.7.0:
- TimelineRows.swift:191-196, confirmationDialog "Edit from this message?": "Revert and keep file changes", then "Revert files too"
  (role .destructive), and a message;
- SettingsView.swift:920-934, confirmationDialog "Delete \"<title>\"?" or "Delete the archived thread?": "Delete thread"
  (.destructive), and a message;
- RootView.swift:80-91, .alert(model.alert.title): "OK" (role .cancel), message model.alert.message;
- ChatView.swift:1231-1237, .alert("Rename thread"): TextField("Title"), "Rename", "Cancel" (.cancel);
- ChatView.swift:1381-1385, .alert("New branch"): TextField("Branch name"), "Create", "Cancel" (.cancel);
- AppUpdater.swift:274-280, NSAlert "Update Failed", warning style, runModal (already on the seam).
Apple documents that every dialog action dismisses the dialog after it runs; that a confirmation dialog includes a standard dismiss
action unless a button has the cancel role, which then takes its place; and that an alert without actions gets a standard "OK".
Today the port has AlertPresentation (src/Marrow.App/Port/AlertPresenter.cs, the updater's plain OK alert) and a private window in
SettingsView.cs:761-772 with no Cancel button. DECISION: AlertPresentation becomes the one seam for all six sites:
- AlertButton gains a Role (None, Cancel, Destructive; SwiftUI ButtonRole), and Show takes the title, an optional message, the
  buttons in declared order, optional text fields (label plus a two-way value) and a kind (Alert or ConfirmationDialog);
- a ConfirmationDialog with no cancel-role button gets a "Cancel" button with that role;
- an Alert with no buttons gets "OK";
- every button runs its action, then closes the dialog;
- Escape and the window's close box run the cancel-role button, or just close when there is none;
- destructive titles draw in Chrome.Danger;
- buttons sit right-aligned in declared order with the cancel-role button moved last (the Windows convention);
- Return activates the first button with no role, and a dialog with no such button has no Return default;
- the title is the window title and a bold first line, and the message and fields follow;
- the dialog is modal, centred on the owner window, and returns a Task that completes on close.
The seam keeps its test override (the Ambient Presenter): tests record the request and press buttons by title, never open a
window. SettingsView's private window, TimelineRows STOP 2, RootView and ChatView all move onto it. ENGINEERING DECISION. macOS's
button order, default-button choice and the look of the sheet stay UNVERIFIED under OD-0001.

ED-217 [UI] Two-line middle truncation (TimelineRows STOP 6). SOURCE FACT: TimelineRows.swift:1969-1973 sets `.lineLimit(2)` and
`.truncationMode(.middle)` on a tool row's label. Every other `.truncationMode(.middle)` site in 1.7.0 is single-line, and those are
served by src/Marrow.UI/Port/MiddleTruncatingText.cs (MiddleTruncatingTextBlock), which is single-line. DECISION:
MiddleTruncatingTextBlock gains a line limit. With a limit of 2, the text wraps normally. When it needs more than two lines, the first
line keeps its normal wrap and the second holds the rest of the text, elided in its own middle to fit the width: the start of the
remainder, U+2026, then the end of the whole string. This is TextKit's rule of truncating only the last line; its exact
middle-truncation of a wrapped paragraph on macOS stays UNVERIFIED under OD-0001. A limit of 1 behaves exactly as today. Tests:
- text that fits in one line or in two is unchanged;
- an overflowing string keeps a whole first line, and its second line ends with the string's own last characters, with one U+2026;
- a limit of 1 is unchanged from today.
ENGINEERING DECISION.

ED-218 [UI][FOUNDATION] ForEach rows enter and leave through their transitions, and surviving rows glide (MCPSettingsPage STOP #4).
SOURCE FACT: 1.7.0 has 136 ForEach sites and 88 .transition(...) sites, many of them rows inside a ForEach under withAnimation or
.animation(_:value:). Examples: MCPSettingsPage.swift:55-57 (the connected grid); TimelineRows.swift:410-414 (FinishedHeadPill with
.settleGlide under .smooth(duration: 0.3)). In SwiftUI, an inserted row plays its insertion transition and a removed row its removal
transition, under the transaction's animation; rows that survive but move animate from their old frame to their new one under the same
transaction. The port's ForEach (src/Marrow.UI/Port/ViewLifetime.cs:88-130) inserts and removes Panel children directly, so none of that
happens. 52 call sites work around it by calling SwiftTransition.Insert/Remove by hand. DECISION: ForEach.Apply does it itself:
- a new row goes in through SwiftTransition.Insert, and a vanished row leaves through SwiftTransition.Remove (it is disposed when its
  removal ends), whenever the row carries a transition (SwiftTransition's attached value) or Transaction.Current is animated;
- rows with no transition and no animated transaction behave exactly as today, so existing callers and tests are unchanged;
- when Transaction.Current is animated, each surviving row whose laid-out position changes is moved FLIP-style: record its bounds
  before Apply; after the next layout pass, set a RenderTransform translation from the old position to the new one and animate it to
  zero with the transaction's curve. Size changes are not animated by this mechanism;
- reduce motion (Transaction.Current already carries it) and window live resize (WindowLiveResize) turn the glide off, as the
  sources gate animations elsewhere.
The 52 hand-written call sites may move to the new ForEach later, but none has to. Tests (headless, clock-driven):
- insert and remove play the row's transition and the removed row is disposed after it;
- a reorder under an animated transaction starts each moved row at its old offset and ends at zero;
- no transition and no animation behaves exactly as before.
ENGINEERING DECISION; SwiftUI's exact interpolation of a moved row stays UNVERIFIED under OD-0001.

ED-219 [WIN][LAUNCH] The Dock unread badge becomes a taskbar overlay badge (AppModel.updateDockBadge). SOURCE FACT: AppModel.swift:1270-1273
sets `NSApp.dockTile.badgeLabel` to the number of threads with hasUnread that are neither archived nor in a panel, or nil when there are
none. The port (AppModel.cs UpdateDockBadge) keeps the count but shows nothing, with a comment that the taskbar cannot show text; no
decision recorded that. Windows has ITaskbarList3::SetOverlayIcon, a small icon drawn over the app's taskbar button, which is how
Windows apps show unread counts. DECISION:
- the port sets the main window's taskbar overlay icon to a badge drawn in code: the count in white on a filled red circle
  (NSColor.systemRed at macOS's light values, the Dock badge's own colours), rendered at the system small-icon size for the current DPI;
- above 99 the badge text stays the decimal count, shrunk to fit, exactly as the source's String(unread) (no "99+" is invented);
- nil clears the overlay;
- the accessible description is the count as text;
- the COM call goes through a seam, so tests record the count and rendered pixels and never touch the real taskbar.
- (owner, 2026-10-02: "Use Inter for the badge digits") the count is set in Inter (OD-0009's face), SemiBold for legibility at
  16 px (the weight is an ENGINEERING DECISION; the source names no badge font), loaded from Avalonia.Fonts.Inter and drawn
  with SkiaSharp so no Avalonia platform is needed.
ENGINEERING DECISION.


## ED-220

[TEST][WIN] Owner-approved collection isolation for process-global Windows native/process proofs.
Authority: R-TEST-5 in IMPLEMENTING.md requires process-global state to stay inside one non-parallel collection. ED-118(6) already applies collection-level DisableParallelization to shared HTTP cookie/cache tests without changing their expectations. The owner explicitly approved this narrow extension on 2026-09-30: exactly the two Windows native/process test collections, preserving all assertions, expectations and test bodies; no new assembly-level, suite-wide or environment parallelism switch.

DECISION: retain the existing CollectionDefinition DisableParallelization=true declarations only for this exception's two named collections:
- WindowManagerNative (tests/Marrow.App.Tests/Fixtures/WindowManagerNativeCollection.cs): the Windows desktop's foreground window, input queues, pointer/keyboard capture and native system menus are process-global resources; each native Fact owns its separate child testhost and STA.
- WindowManager process proof (tests/Marrow.App.Tests/Fixtures/WindowManagerProcessCollection.cs): the parent pins and observes the owned child test process while the selected child owns its HeadlessSession. Collection isolation protects process/native-host proof ownership.

This approval does not serialize the whole assembly or suite, authorize an environment switch, or permit hiding a hang, blocked dialog, process leak or deadlock. The existing App MaxParallelThreads=4 remains unchanged; Headless has no DisableParallelization flag. Other eligible collections run in parallel outside these exclusive collections, and the ordinary six-group runner remains parallel. No production source, test body, assertion or expectation changes accompany this decision.

VERIFICATION: independent E accepted source/test tree 03481b8cd0ba418f95840eeb2879d22b5d319ea2 conditioned only on this documentation and unchanged code. After owner-notified hands-off/other-PC-control pause, WindowManagerNative passed 19/19 twice with fresh data and all 19 API-key variables removed; foreground before both runs was ChatGPT PID88252. All 1952 source/test hashes match. The explicit owner-authorized combined gate counts the 19 native cases once alongside exact-tree prior five-group and 1396 non-native App-rest evidence: 12247 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped. It is combined evidence, not a new monolithic green run. No full-suite rerun is required for this documentation-only decision and no whole-record status advances are claimed.

The external lane brief E:/Droppy/work/codex/turbo/codex_common.md gains the matching narrow collection-exception line; its ban on serialization to hide hangs remains. ENGINEERING DECISION; owner-approved test isolation, not a behavior deviation or a new parity claim.


## ED-227

[DOC][WIN][LAUNCH] Restored Windows toast mechanism; historical citation mapping only.
Provenance: the original seven-part toast decision was recorded as ED-220 in commit
168b20c0582cf235af24bf8f4efc8630b8c52bd0 (2026-09-27), porting/engineering_decisions.md.
Its owner authority is OD-0028 from f4db0ef539f50bfe6bcc8cbfc59e367f9fc562f1,
restored verbatim in porting/owner_decisions.md. This recovers existing authority; it grants no new
permission, changes no behavior and claims no runtime verification.

LEGACY MAPPING: toast references to ED-220 (1)-(7), including WindowsToastPlatform.cs:3
(1)-(3), (6)-(7), WindowsToastNotifications.cs, WindowsToastLaunchTransport.cs and ToastIcon.cs,
mean ED-227 with the same numbered clauses below. The current ED-220 is the separately approved
Windows native/process collection exception and is preserved verbatim; it is not toast authority.
Only the historical toast identifier is disambiguated here. The original source facts and seven
numbered decisions follow without substantive changes; runtime source comments remain untouched.

[WIN][LAUNCH] Windows toasts for AppModel.notify, UpdateChecker.notifyOnce and the notification delegate (OD-0028; audit G1-03).
SOURCE FACT:
- AppModel.swift:1248-1266 notify: skipped when the app is active and the thread is on screen; asks permission once; content title,
  body and sound (.default, or nil at :1215); userInfo ["threadID": uuidString]; the request identifier is the thread's uuidString,
  so a newer notification for the same thread replaces the older one.
- UpdateChecker.swift:245-261 notifyOnce: userInfo ["update": version].
- AppDelegate.swift:63-75 willPresent: nothing while the app is active and the notified thread is selected; otherwise banner and sound.
- AppDelegate.swift:77-90 didReceive: show main unless it is an update; select the thread; activate; for an update, Settings > About.
The port posted nothing: AppModel.Notify was a no-op and UpdateToastCenter defaulted to NoUpdateToastCenter.
DECISION:
1. Only Marrow.App targets net10.0-windows10.0.19041.0, for Microsoft's WinRT projection (OD-0028). Toasts go through
   Windows.UI.Notifications ToastNotificationManager.
2. Identity. The app sets an explicit AppUserModelID at start, before any window:
   - "MarrowCode.Marrow" for a release build, and "MarrowCode.Marrow.Dev" for a debug build or a build run with MARROW_DEV_DATA_ROOT
     (ED-212 naming);
   - it registers per user under HKCU\Software\Classes\AppUserModelId\<id>, with DisplayName "Marrow" and IconUri set to the app icon,
     writing only when a value differs;
   - these names never equal or read those of the owner's separate "Marrow" Electron app.
3. Posting. A ToastGeneric toast with two texts, the title and the body; the default sound, or <audio silent="true"/> when the source
   passes nil; Tag set to the request identifier, so a newer toast replaces an older one as the source's identifiers do; and the
   userInfo carried in the activation arguments.
4. requestNotificationPermission stays a once-only step with no prompt, because Windows has none. The user's Windows notification
   setting for the app governs.
5. Foreground rule. The willPresent logic (:63-75) runs just before posting. When it returns nothing, no toast is shown: Windows has no
   per-toast foreground hook, so deciding first gives the same visible result.
6. Activation. The toast uses protocol activation with a per-user URI scheme ("marrow-code-<build identity>:", registered in HKCU at
   start, internal plumbing never shown to the user), so a click works whether or not the app is running.
   - A click on a running app goes through ED-002's second-launch path to the running instance, carrying the payload. If that path
     forwards no arguments today, it gains a payload message.
   - The running instance then does exactly what didReceive (:77-90) does.
7. Every Windows call (AUMID, registry, ToastNotifier, the URI scheme) goes through a seam. Tests record the requests and never post a
   real toast, write the real registry or launch a URI.
ENGINEERING DECISION; toast visuals are Windows' own.

## ED-228

Authority: PORT_CONTRACT.md/source precedence and the pinned B3 52bc792
App/Views/Composer/ComposerWorkingDots.swift:5-11,67-79,104-149,152-190. The source
places this CALayer/CAReplicatorLayer field's steady animation on the render server,
without timers, view updates or main-thread drawing. Independent E accepted the
five-path partial implementation on 2026-09-30 under manifest SHA256
80F7AE84A513D7FAFFA55385E123BB594472088791873C0FDC825E35D215DC01.

For this field alone, CompositionCustomVisualHandler's compositor animation-frame
callbacks provide steady-state wake-ups. Elapsed time still comes from the captured
SwiftClock.Provider and its SwiftClock timestamp conversion; Avalonia's animation
time does not determine phase or duration. The shared pulse origin and source
constants remain intact. Lifecycle, motion, color, appearance and layout changes
remain on the actual Avalonia main executor under OD-0034/amended ED-065; immutable
state crosses to the compositor, which does not dispatch or mutate UI controls.
Other FrameClock, DisplayLink, TimelineView and frame-paced task users retain
ED-098/ED-117 unchanged. This is a source-specific platform adaptation, not a new
product deviation or a suite-wide clock exception.

Evidence scope: 29 headless cases, old-renderer regression red twice, six mutants
red twice each with restored 29-case greens, fourteen bindings restored, and all
22 invocations checking 19 process keys absent with unique fresh data. The finite
sweep endpoint is compared in the existing TimeSpan clock domain; no source timing
constant, test expectation or timeout changes. Headless rendering does not prove
production off-UI render-thread ownership. PR-COMPOSER-103, T-M7-086 and capture
parity/UI-COMPOSER-017 remain open; no record or packet status advances here.

## ED-230

[WIN][SHORTCUTS] How the "+" key equivalent is pressed (STOP App.AppCommands #2). AppCommands.swift:53-54 gives Zoom In the literal key equivalent "+" with Command, and :59-62 adds a hidden "=" item because "US keyboards produce '=' for Command-plus without Shift". On a Mac a menu key equivalent matches the character the key types, so Cmd-Shift-= and the keypad + reach "+". The port reads key events as US key positions (ED-099), which never produce "+", so on Windows the "+" item was unreachable (Ctrl+Shift+= and Ctrl+numpad + did nothing). DECISION: `MenuKeyEquivalents.Plus` reads Shift with the "=" key, and the numeric keypad's + (with or without Shift), as the key equivalent "+" with the other modifiers held, Shift removed because it is part of typing "+". The window dispatch offers the chord as its key position first and offers the "+" reading only when no command took the chord, so a user shortcut bound to Ctrl+Shift+= keeps working. Only "+" is read this way: the other keypad keys are left out because no source item needs them and reading them as digits would change which commands Ctrl+keypad-digit reaches. Tests: AppCommandsFinishTests (Decision ED-230).

## ED-231

[UI][MAC-LOOK] How OD-0042 ("Mac look, native menu") and OD-0045 ("Use Apple's design kits") are carried out for the push buttons, the rounded-border text field and the help tag. The values come from Apple's "Apple macOS 27 UI Kit" (Sketch web share named in OD-0054), read through its Inspect panel on 2026-10-02 and recorded with symbol ids in `E:\Droppy\work\apple-kit\macos27-uikit-controls.md`; each is a SOURCE FACT (Apple design resource). DECISION: (1) `SystemButtons` draws `.bordered` / `.borderedProminent` at `.controlSize(.regular)`, the size every site sets (QuestionTab.swift:165, SidebarView.swift:1018): 24 high, padding 16 / 4, radius 6, no border, label medium 13 / 16; bordered fill #000000@0.08 / #FFFFFF@0.07, 0.16 while pressed, 0.04 disabled with a Labels 3 Tertiary label; prominent fill the accent with a white label, a #000000@0.1 / #FFFFFF@0.1 wash while pressed, the fill at 40 % and the label at 50 % when disabled; no hover state (the kit has none); keyboard focus draws a 3.5 pt accent@0.25 band outside the bezel. (2) The `.roundedBorder` field (ChatDialogControls) is 24 high, radius 6, fill #FFFFFF / #1E1E1E, a 1 px #000000@0.05 / #FFFFFF@0.04 border, the text 6 in from each side; keyboard focus adds the same 3.5 pt accent@0.25 band as a spread shadow. (3) The `.help` tag (PortControlThemes) is padded 6 / 3 with square corners, fill #E7E7E7@0.85 / #262626@0.8, shadows 0 0 2 #000000@0.4 and 0 2 8 #000000@0.2 plus a 0.6 inner #FFFFFF@0.15 hairline in Dark, text medium 11 / 13 in #4C4C4C / #FFFFFF@0.96. Port choices: the accent stands for System Blue (the app's tint governs prominent buttons); the kit's "smooth" corners are drawn as circular arcs (OD-0005); the kit's outside field border is drawn inside the 24-point frame with the padding giving back the point; plus-lighter / plus-darker text blending is drawn as normal blending; the tag's 45-point background blur is not drawn (a tooltip is its own popup; OD-0005) and the tag keeps 8 / 8 / 8 / 10 points of room inside its popup so its shadows are not clipped. Replaces the Windows 11 buttons, text box and tooltip of the ED-229 proposal; the native context menu stays (OD-0042). (4) The indeterminate `ProgressView()` (SystemSpinner) is the kit's spinner: eight capsule spokes every 45 degrees, 4 x 10 spanning 6 to 16 from the centre at 32 points and half that at 16 (the size the sites use), white in Dark and black in Light, the lead spoke at 0.55 and the others clockwise 0.06, 0.13 ... 0.48; the lead steps one spoke clockwise every eighth of a 1 s period (the period is UNVERIFIED: the kit is static). The small slider follows in a later step. Tests: SystemButtonsTests, ToolTipThemeTests, SystemSpinnerTests (Decision ED-231), QuestionTabTests (PR-COMPOSER-193, UI-COMPOSER-075).

## ED-232

[UI][FRAMES] Amends ED-117 (2)-(4) for TimelineView (OD-0059). A timeline with a minimum interval draws when the span since its previous *due time* is complete (elapsed + 1 ms), and its next due time is that due time plus the interval; a timeline more than two intervals behind (a pause, a slow frame) takes the frame it is at as its new start. Before, the span ran from the moment the previous draw happened to run, so a frame callback's jitter made a 1/60 timeline skip every other frame of a ~60 Hz frame clock (native run 2026-10-02 on the owner's PC: 33 updates a second). The average rate never exceeds the interval. A timeline also re-reads its schedule when its view's inherited \.accessibilityReduceMotion changes (ED-084: an Avalonia property that observation tracking does not see), so Reduce Motion turned on at run time pauses a running timeline. Native evidence: EffortSliderNativeFrameTests (real window, real frame clock): the track takes every update ED-232 allows over the frames that come and never more than 60 a second. UNRESOLVED: on the owner's 240 Hz display Avalonia's frame clock delivers 4 ms frames broken by frequent 21-29 ms stalls (about 80 frames a second on average), so the frames allow about 48 updates a second; the stalls are Avalonia's and not yet explained (composition mode, timer resolution and rendering mode probes made no difference). Tests: FrameClockTests (five rewritten with the new due times), TimelineViewEnvironmentTests, EffortSliderSweepTests.

## ED-233

[UI][LIQUID] The liquid tube is drawn in small GPU passes. The single shader (content() three times for the refraction, each with the currents, caustic, oil and 24 bubbles inlined) overflowed the native stack of ANGLE's D3D shader compile on Avalonia's render thread: with the default rendering mode (AngleEgl) the process crashed (0xC00000FD) the first time a liquid track drew on a real window; headless tests never saw it because they rasterise on the CPU. Bisected natively: every part compiled alone, the combination did not; WGL, Vulkan and Software did not crash. DECISION: keep AngleEgl and compose the liquid once into an offscreen surface at device scale: (A) the breathing gradient, the oil (screen), the currents (soft light), the slow current (soft light), the caustic (overlay) and the oil for one model (screen) as separate shaders blended with Skia's own W3C separable blend modes (the canvas's mix-blend-modes), each bubble as its own small shader on its own rectangle, then the capsule coverage (DstIn); (B) a glass shader samples that surface three times through the displacement map for the per-channel refraction and adds the gloss and rims. The maths of every layer is unchanged; the layers now meet through an 8-bit surface instead of float registers. The ?: chains over half4 became flat if/else chains (they also tripped the compile). Evidence: the 157 headless slider and liquid tests (pixel checks included) pass unchanged; EffortSliderNativeFrameTests draws every liquid look on the real GPU and finds its colour on screen. Also roughly a third of the per-pixel work of the one-shader form.


## ED-234

[PROVIDERS][OPENROUTER] OpenRouter as an API-key provider, engine only (OD-0049, OD-0060). PORT-ONLY: the source has no OpenRouter provider (only PiCLI.swift:38 passes OPENROUTER_API_KEY through to Pi); it is built in the manner of the source's OpenAI-compatible providers (DeepSeek, Meta, Z.ai: OpenAICompatibleAPI/OpenAICompatibleSession, ProviderRegistry.loadAPICatalog/refreshAPIProvider, APIKeychain). The model picker and its search field wait for the owner's approval of the canvas (OD-0060), so no screen or control is added. DECISION: (1) `ProviderKind.OpenRouter`, raw value `openrouter`, declared after `pi` so the fourteen source cases keep their places (the case name is the brand's spelling; R-NAME-2 would give `Openrouter`). Members: display name "OpenRouter"; no executable (""); login command `OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...`; install page https://openrouter.ai/keys; isAPIKeyBased and acceptsAPIKey; apiHost `openrouter.ai/api/v1`; apiKeySource `openrouter.ai/keys`; apiKeyEnvVar `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`; supportsCompact and supportsImages true; not ACP, no rewind; icon name `provider-openrouter` (no mark is shipped yet, so the icon draws empty until the owner supplies or approves one). (2) The key lives in the Credential Manager under the account "OpenRouter API Key" (APIKeychain), edited through `AppSettings.OpenRouterAPIKeyInput` (refusal line, clearing and trimming as the four others), and `ApiKey(.openrouter)` falls back to the environment variable. The Settings -> Providers page already has a section per provider, so OpenRouter appears there with the key row, eye and "Get a ... key" link DeepSeek has. (3) `OpenRouterAPI`: base https://openrouter.ai/api/v1; `Validate` is GET /key with the bearer key (the models endpoint answers 200 without a key, so it cannot prove one; UNVERIFIED: written from OpenRouter's public API reference and never called from here); `ListModels` is GET /models with the bearer key. (4) The catalogue parses id, name, context_length, pricing.prompt/completion (USD per token, as strings), architecture.input_modalities and supported_parameters. A row is the id, the name without its "Vendor: " lead (the id names the vendor, and the composer's chip name cuts a name at that colon), a detail "vendor · 200K context · $3 / $15 per 1M" (free when both prices are 0, no price when a price is absent or negative, as the auto router's -1 is), the efforts low/medium/high with default medium for a model whose parameters include reasoning or include_reasoning, and `openrouter/auto` as the default row. The list is ordered default first then by id, as OpenAICompatibleAPI.ListModels orders it; rows without an id are dropped; a non-200 answer or an empty list is an empty catalogue; a transport failure throws and the registry swallows it as for the other providers. It is cached by the registry exactly as the others are (ProviderRegistry.UpdateCatalog under providerModelCatalogs with the date under providerModelCatalogDates, read back at init), seeded offline with the router row alone (`OpenRouterSeed`), loaded once per launch for a configured key (AppModel launch, LoadAPICatalog) and forced when a key is typed in Settings. `ProviderRegistry.Models(.openrouter)` is the list the composer's picker reads for every provider; the search UI is not built. ModelOption has no field for a context length or an image ability, so the last list fetched is also kept in memory (`OpenRouterAPI.ContextWindow`, `IsVisionModel`; 128,000 and false until a list has loaded). (5) `OpenRouterSession` is an OpenAICompatibleSession: POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions with the bearer key, tools and tool_choice auto, `stream_options.include_usage`, and the effort as `reasoning: {effort}` (low, medium, high; xhigh, extra-high and max send high; anything else sends none); reasoning is read from delta.reasoning and not replayed; the usage ring measures against the model's own context length (base-class hook `ContextWindowFor`, default unchanged for the other providers); refusals are put in words by status and message (401, 402 credits, no endpoint serving the model, a model without tool use, 429, context length, timeout). No HTTP-Referer or X-Title attribution headers are sent. Status check: no key is signed out with nothing asked of the network; a key GET /key accepts is signed in, "API", key configured; a rejected key is signed out but still counts as installed. OpenRouter exposes no plan limits and no credits. (6) The slider brand is `EffortBrand.Purple`, the source's no-provider default, marked "OD-0050 pending: automatic colour". (7) Not built, for the owner: the picker UI and its search; an OpenRouter mark; a balance panel (GET /credits); a Settings search keyword for the page (the source's list is pinned by UI-PROVREG-001); "Get a OpenRouter key" is the generic row's wording. Tests (Decision ED-234): ProviderOpenRouterTests, OpenRouterAPITests, OpenRouterSessionTests, OpenRouterRegistryTests, OpenRouterKeyStoreTests, AppSettingsOpenRouterTests, EffortBrandOpenRouterTests, ThreadRuntimeOpenRouterSessionTests, SettingsProviderOpenRouterTests; every request is answered in process through URLSession.Transport (OD-0057) and every key is made up. Existing tests that closed the provider set at fourteen were widened to say "the fourteen source cases, plus OpenRouter".
## ED-235

[BUILD][INSTALLER] Release preparation builds a Velopack per-user install (OD-0062), LOCAL ONLY (OD-0058): nothing is signed, uploaded, published, released or pushed, and the produced installer is never run on a development PC (Setup.exe installs the app). DECISION: (1) Directory.Packages.props pins `Velopack` 1.2.161, equal to the `vpk` tool version (`dotnet tool install -g vpk --version 1.2.161`; vpk checks the library in the app and the script refuses a mismatched tool); Marrow.App references it. (2) Program.Main's first statement is `RunVelopackHook(AppContext.BaseDirectory)`, before RestoreDevRoot, the single-instance lock and every binding, so the Update.exe hook runs (`--veloapp-install`, `-updated`, `-obsolete`, `-uninstall`: Velopack handles the event and exits the process) before the app does anything. It calls `VelopackApp.Build().Run()` only in a Velopack install (Update.exe one folder above the app's own folder, Velopack's layout); review fix: Velopack's Run() writes %LOCALAPPDATA%\velopack\velopack.log on every call, installed or not (seen on this PC from the first version of the tests), so a dev run or a test host never calls Velopack at all. An installed app started normally: Run() returns at once. Defaults are kept (auto-apply of an already-downloaded newer package on start stays on; nothing downloads one yet). The existing AppUpdater, UpdateChecker, UpdateInstallBoundary and the feed value of OD-0008 I1 are unchanged; how they meet UpdateManager is a proposal in the build report, not decided here. (3) `scripts/package-windows.ps1` runs `dotnet publish src/Marrow.App -c Release -r win-x64 --self-contained` into artifacts/publish and `vpk pack` into artifacts/releases (both gitignored): app id `MarrowCode`, title "Marrow Code", main exe Marrow.App.exe, icon Assets/icon.ico, authors "Marrow", Start menu shortcut only, no `--signParams`. Identity: the id installs to `%LOCALAPPDATA%\MarrowCode` (Velopack's own layout, current/ and packages/) beside, never inside, the data folder `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Marrow Code` (OD-0008 C7); the title is "Marrow Code" (not "Marrow") because OD-0008 C7 names the Start menu entry "Marrow Code" and a plain "Marrow" would collide with the owner's Electron app Marrow. (4) Versioning: no new scheme. The script reads the existing version source, the `CFBundleShortVersionString` assembly metadata in src/Marrow.App/AssemblyInfo.cs (1.7.0; AppInfo.Version reads the same), as Velopack's version; CFBundleVersion (the build number, 21) has no Velopack field and is not encoded. A release newer than 1.7.0 needs that metadata raised first. Evidence: the script ran once locally (Release publish, 232 files, 245 MB; Setup.exe 71.2 MB, full nupkg 63.6 MB, a portable zip and the feed files); vpk itself reported it verified VelopackApp.Run() in Program.Main. Not done: signing (vpk warns that 225 files are unsigned), a feed, delta packages (none until a second release is packed), a run of the installer. Tests (Trait Decision ED-235): VelopackStartupHookTests (Main's first two calls, read from its IL, are AppContext.BaseDirectory and RunVelopackHook; only the Velopack layout counts as installed; a run Velopack did not install leaves velopack.log untouched and sets no locator; removing the guard fails the last test). The installed case cannot be tested without installing: Run() exits the process for a hook argument. AMENDED by ED-247 (OD-0072): the title is "Marrow" (no longer "Marrow Code"), the authors "Marrow Code" and the shortcut `StartMenu` (Start Menu\Programs\Marrow Code\Marrow.lnk, never the Start menu root, where the owner's Electron app has Marrow.lnk); the app id MarrowCode and the install folder are unchanged; the installer to share is the version gate artifacts/installer/Marrow-<version>-Setup.exe around vpk's Setup.exe.

## ED-236

[WIN][GLASS][LAUNCH] The clear windows blur what is behind them, and the boot hand-over hides the Acrylic's start-up (OD-0005, OD-0014, OD-0041; closes WindowManager STOP #5). DEFECT (native launch capture 2026-10-02): the main window and the tour window were clear windows with no backdrop (Background Transparent; the tour's hint was Transparent), so other windows' text showed through sharp and the tour's text collided with the main window's text under it; on the Mac both are `.glassEffect(.regular, ...)` over a clear NSWindow, which blurs what is behind it (WindowChrome.swift:116-117, TourWindowController.swift:82-83, TourView.swift:79-86). (1) BACKDROP. `WindowChrome.GlassBackdrop` is `[AcrylicBlur, Transparent]` (Avalonia takes the first level the platform supports; Acrylic alone would end as an opaque black window where unsupported, P3's `ctl_none_opaque`). `WindowChrome.Configure` sets it beside the transparent Background, which reaches the main and Settings windows through WindowManager.MakeWindow (:101); `TourWindowController` sets it in place of Transparent. The app-drawn tint and scrim (Chrome.WindowBackdrop, SwiftGlass, the tour card's tint and scrim) stay exactly as ported, over the window's blur, as P3 requires (Avalonia's recipe adds no tint: mean shift 1.3). Checked against the Swift for every top-level window: the main and Settings windows (WindowBackdrop, RootView.swift:64, SettingsView.swift:118), the tour (TourView.swift:79-86) and the two floating guide panels (MCPKeyPanel.swift:56, MCPSetupPanel.swift:130, already AcrylicBlur in FloatingGuidePanel.cs) are glass over a clear window; the boot stage (OD-0018, deliberately a click-through transparent overlay) and the attachment-flight overlay (AttachmentFlight.swift:133-134, a clear overlay window, not glass) are not, and keep Transparent. (2) HAND-OVER (OD-0041). Probes P13 and P14 (`porting/probes/p14/RESULT.md`): a plainly shown Acrylic window of the factory kind has its tint at about +80 ms and its blur at about +313 ms (15 of 95 samples tinted-over-sharp, about 230 ms); `Window.Opacity = 0`, a layered alpha 0 and a position off the screen do NOT hide the Acrylic (it shows as a frosted pane); DWM cloaking does: a window shown cloaked (DWMWA_CLOAK) displays nothing, is composed by DWM meanwhile, and on uncloak its first displayed frame is already blurred and tinted (0 tinted-but-sharp samples of 47, after a cloak of 0, 300 or 1200 ms). DECISION: `BootStageWindow` (stage already covering the work area, ED-103) shows the main window early and cloaked, as the disintegration begins (BootPhase.Disintegrating, the outline lands at least 0.8 s later; with reduce motion 0.5 s before the fixed 2.5 s hand-over), cloaked before it is shown and shown without activation (ShowActivated false for that one Show, then restored), its root content following the stage's opacity and scale from then on (ED-103 (5)); at ED-103 (5)'s hand-over it uncloaks the window (the content already at that frame's value) and only then runs the launch's show (WindowManager.ShowMain: Show, Activate), so the activation, the OD-0040 first-activation check and the 700 ms tour/About timers are unchanged. `WindowCloak.Set` is DwmSetWindowAttribute(13) and returns false for a window without a Win32 handle or when DWM refuses; then nothing is shown early and the hand-over is the plain show of before. If the stage closes with the window still cloaked it is uncloaked. Scope: the boot hand-over only; no other window is cloaked. (3) NATIVE EVIDENCE (`GlassWindowNativeTests`, real windows, real composed screen pixels over a window of 6 px black and white stripes; contrast = mean absolute luma step, 42.9 sharp, 0 blurred): the factory main window with the test scrim black at 66/255: 42.86 behind it bare, 0.00 under it active, mean 127.5 to 94.0 (127.5 x (1 - 0.2588) = 94.5), and 0.00 / 94.0 again when another window of the process is active, so Avalonia's Acrylic does not flatten when inactive (it matches P3, and OD-0014 asks only for the material over the desktop; what the Mac glass does inactive is not established, P3). The tour card: 43.22 bare, 0.00 after, mean 127.5 to 76.0, and no frame of it was tinted over sharp stripes in 3 runs (its window is borderless: P14's `window0-borderless` row, the gap is the framed windows' first show). The boot hand-over with reduce motion: without it 47 to 49 sampled frames (192 to 200 ms) are the scrim over sharp stripes; with it 0 of about 420 to 470, nothing of the main window shows before the hand-over (all samples within 1.5 of the bare stripes while the window had been shown cloaked for 0.5 s), and the first changed sample is the blur (127.0 / 0.00, the scrim then fades in with the content); full sequence: 0 tinted-over-sharp frames from the hand-over on (before it the sampled block is crossed by window particles, which the strict check cannot judge: one run showed a particle at 125.0 / 40.0). Eight mutants of the code were each killed by at least two tests (no hint; tour Transparent; the early show off for the reduce-motion branch alone and for both branches; no uncloak; the early show without the cloak; the launch's show before the uncloak; an activating early show). UNRESOLVED (named, not hidden): (a) CORNERS: an Acrylic window is a rectangle (DWM rounds it by 8 px) while the content draws a 26 pt shape (Chrome.windowCornerRadius, the tour card 20 pt): the wedge between the shape and the window shows the Acrylic without the scrim, measured luma 126 beside 93 inside the shape, about 7 px deep on the diagonal at 100 % for the main window and a darker gradient (the card's shadow) for the tour. On the Mac the corner outside the shape is clear. SetWindowRgn did not clip the Acrylic (the window went square and lost its shadow, probed 2026-10-02). Options that need an owner ruling: leave it, fill the wedge with the scrim, or DwmSetWindowAttribute(DWMWCP_ROUND) for the borderless tour (8 px). (b) A Settings window opened by the user shows the same 225 ms gap on its first show (55 frames, 3 runs; a second show has none; measured, not fixed: OD-0041 names the boot sequence and a cloak-then-uncloak in WindowManager.Present removes it, at the cost of the system's window-appear animation). (c) Whether a cloaked, shown window has a taskbar button was not checked (the main window may appear in the taskbar up to about a second before it is displayed). (d) The measurements are one PC (RTX 4080, 100 %, dark, transparency effects on); light theme, another DPI, a second monitor, effects off are untested. Tests: WindowChromeAcrylicTests, WindowManagerTests (the main and Settings windows), TourWindowAcrylicTests, BootStageWindowTests (the four ED-236 tests), GlassWindowNativeTests (the WindowManagerNative collection; its class is on WindowManagerNativeChildProtocol.FactName's allow-list), Trait Decision ED-236.

## ED-237

[UI][FRAMES] The frame source keeps Avalonia's render loop on the display's refresh while frames are requested (OD-0052: the liquid track never below 60; amends ED-117 (1)'s "frames are the only wake-ups" only in how a frame is obtained). Found natively on the owner's 240 Hz display (STOP EffortSlider native #1): Avalonia 12.1.2's render loop goes idle after a frame that changes nothing on screen, and the next TopLevel.RequestAnimationFrame then waits for the idle wake-up (16-31 ms) instead of the next refresh. A TimelineView at 1/60 draws on one refresh in four there, so three frames in four changed nothing and the track got about 48 updates a second. Probe (5 s each, native child windows): a window requesting frames and changing nothing, 40 frames/s with 199 gaps over 15 ms; one repainting a brush every frame, 240/s and none; the liquid tube, 81/s and 165; GC pause 0 ms in all, so not the collector. Composition mode, a 1 ms system timer and the rendering mode had not changed it (2026-10-02). DECISION: AvaloniaFrameSource.RequestFrame also calls the window's Compositor.RequestCommitAsync(); an empty commit draws nothing but keeps the loop ticking on the display's refresh. With it: the unchanging window 240/s, the liquid tube 240/s, no gap over 15 ms; the track's updates are ED-232's 60 a second. Cost: one commit per refresh, only while some view requests frames (a running TimelineView, a display link); an idle window requests none. Evidence: EffortSliderNativeFrameTests now also requires at least 58 updates a second; removing the commit request fails the solo and fast-track runs (mutation checked).

## ED-238

[UI][THEME] A dark app drew its popovers as white cards, and an accent that does not read on the window vanished (native gallery, E:\Droppy\work\gallery, 2026-10-02: composer-model-picker-dark.png, composer-effort-*-dark.png, main-thread-popover-diff-dark.png; main-thread-2-dark.png and -light.png links; settings-general-dark.png "Daily"). Three causes, all found by reading Avalonia 12.1.2 and by a headless reproduction, none by guessing. (1) A Popup opens a PopupRoot, a separate top-level whose ActualThemeVariant is bound to the Popup's (Popup.Open); a Popup takes its variant from its logical parent, and Avalonia gives one a parent only for a flyout, a tooltip or a menu (Popup.SetPopupParent, internal). Every site of this port builds `new Popup { PlacementTarget = anchor }` and never adds it to a tree, so the popup inherited nothing, the root's variant was null and the content (Chrome colours, the labelColor default of PortControlThemes) resolved Light inside a dark app. (2) PopupRoot's default Background is opaque white (its static constructor), in both appearances. (3) The accent is the Windows personalization accent (ED-051, ED-092) and Windows lets the user pick any colour: the owner's is #000000 (HKCU DWM AccentColor 0xFF000000), so every accent use (the link colour LinkParagraphView.swift:485-489, the selected chip Components.swift:84-85, the prominent buttons, the toggles) was black on the dark glass; AppKit's accent is always a colour that reads (Graphite is a mid grey, every accent a little brighter in Dark). DECISION: (1) PopoverHost.Prepare, called by the presenter (Presentation) before it opens a popup, gives the popup its PlacementTarget as logical parent, as Avalonia's own flyout does, and takes it back when the popup closes, so the popup and its top-level inherit the anchor's appearance; it also puts the style class `marrow-popover` on the popup. (2) An application style (PortControlThemes.Register through PopoverHost.Register) gives the PopupRoot of such a popup the macOS 27 UI Kit's panel for popovers' plain panels, SOURCE FACT (Apple design resource, OD-0045; E:\Droppy\workpple-kit\macos27-uikit-controls.md "Panels"): Dark fill #1E1E1E with a 1 px #FFFFFF at 0.2 border, Light fill #FFFFFF with no visible edge (the kit's shadows are the window manager's: not drawn here). A tooltip is a Popup too and keeps its own clear surround (TipTemplate): only a popover the presenter shows gets the panel. (3) SwiftColor.Resolve keeps the Windows accent unless it has under 3:1 contrast (WCAG 2.x, the contrast Windows asks of UI components) against the appearance's window background (the kit's Window backgrounds: Dark #1E1E1E, Light #FFFFFF); then it is mixed toward white in Dark and toward black in Light by the smallest 1/255 step that reaches 3:1. An opaque black accent therefore reads as #686868 on Dark and stays black on Light; every accent that already reads (the headless #0078D7: 3.6:1 and 4.5:1) and every theme's own accent (AppTheme.Accent, which does not go through the system accent) is untouched. A new internal seam, SwiftColor.AccentSource, is where the system accent is read from (the platform's by default) so a test can stand for such a PC. UNRESOLVED (named, not hidden): on a black accent the Light appearance still draws links and the selected chip in black, as Swift would with that accent, so a link there is a bold black word; whether an achromatic accent should instead be drawn as Graphite (a mid grey) is an owner choice (a different accent in Windows Settings > Personalization > Colors also removes it). Not drawn: the popover panel's rounded corners and shadow (a native Win32 popup is a rectangle; OD-0005). Tests: PopoverHostThemeTests (the presenter's adoption and release; a PopupRoot built as Popup.Open builds it, headless returning no popup implementation, by HeadlessPopupHost: dark and light card, border, label and secondary text, a switch to Light; a tooltip untouched), AccentLegibilityTests, LinkAccentLegibilityTests, TokenActivityChipLegibilityTests, Decision ED-238; mutation checked (each of: no Prepare in the presenter, no adoption, no class, no style, no legibility step fails its tests).

## ED-242

[TERM][WIN] The CTRL_BREAK helper never outlives its work (amends the helper of ED-047 / ED-126 and probe P6 as ProcessNative.SendCtrlBreak built it; the ladders, their deadlines and Terminate returning at once are unchanged). DEFECT: 52 helpers (powershell.exe running the MarrowCtrlBreak script) were found alive on this PC, orphaned and idle, the oldest a day old. Two causes, each reproduced (2026-10-02, scratch programs, nothing in the app): (1) ORPHANED SUSPENDED. When the creating process ends inside CreateProcessW, between the creation of the process (first thread suspended) and its resume, the helper stays suspended for ever with no parent: one thread in Wait/Suspended, about 2 to 3 MB, no CPU, no console host (the 52 matched: ~1.8 MB, 0 CPU). A process launching helpers on four threads and exiting under them left 29 such orphans in 20 runs; one appeared from a Marrow.Services.Tests run, created at 16:14:44, the second its test host ended. (2) DEBUGGER STRAND. A CTRL_BREAK that reaches a helper while Windows PowerShell is starting on its hidden console puts it in the script debugger ("Entering debug mode. Use h or ? for help." and a [DBG] prompt, read back from the helper's console) waiting for input for ever, or ends it with 0xC000013A before it sent its own event. The helper led a process group named by its own pid (CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP), so any process attaching to its console by that pid and sending CTRL_BREAK to that group reached it, which is exactly what a helper sent for a stale pid does once the system has given that pid to a new helper: a sender attaching 80 to 160 ms into a helper's start stranded 3 of 15 and killed 6; against a helper leading no group, 30 of 30 untouched (GenerateConsoleCtrlEvent fails with 87). Stale pids are common: instrumented, 159 of the 194 helpers of one Services suite run (and 10 of 48 over four Core runs) were sent for a child that had already exited, its exit not yet seen by the watcher. Ruled out by experiment: a target that has exited, has no console, dies before or after the helper attaches, is killed with its job (console host included) while the helper is attached, is not a group leader, or ignores the break; the helper's own exit after FreeConsole with null standard handles; a CTRL_BREAK reaching the helper while attached to the target's console (it ends with 0xC000013A, no hang). DECISION: (a) the helper is created inside a job of its own with JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE, assigned at creation (PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST), whose only handle is the app's: if the app ends at any point of the launch the system closes that handle and the job ends the helper; once CreateProcessW has returned the limit is cleared, so a running helper still finishes its one call after the app has quit, as before. (b) The helper no longer starts a process group (CREATE_NO_WINDOW only; it is in the app's group): an event for the group of its pid reaches nobody, and it is still never in its target's group. P6 created its helper with DETACHED_PROCESS; Windows PowerShell created that way exits 0 at once without running its command (measured), so the helper keeps its hidden console. (c) Terminate hands the helper a duplicate of the child's process handle, held until the helper has ended, so the target's pid cannot be given to another process before the helper attaches (no process, helper or not, receives an event meant for an exited child). (d) A background thread waits for the helper for at most 10 s (CtrlBreakHelper.Lifetime: PowerShell starts in about 0.3 s idle and was seen over 3 s under load; the bound is above the ladders' 1 s and 3 s kill steps, which still run from the call), then TerminateProcess, and closes the helper, job and reservation handles. Tests (Decision ED-242): ProcessLauncherCtrlBreakHelperTests (a helper whose creator lets go of it before its launch completes ends with the creator's handles (a job ends a suspended process the same way; src keeps no CREATE_SUSPENDED, ProcessLauncherTests' scan); a stranded helper ends at its lifetime; a CTRL_BREAK for the group of a starting helper's pid reaches nobody; a launched helper still finishes when its creator lets go; the reservation holds the exited child's pid until the helper is let go; a cooperating child still ends with 131 on the CTRL_BREAK; helpers sent to an exited child, a child killed while the helper starts and a child that ignores the break all end by themselves). Against the previous behaviour four of them fail; each of the five parts reverted alone (bounded wait, no group, kill-on-close at creation, reservation, limit cleared after the launch) fails at least one (mutation checked). End to end: a process calling SendCtrlBreak on four threads and exiting under them left 0 orphans in 40 runs (the previous launch, same flags and no job, from the same harness: 29 and 55 in two sets of 20). The existing signal, spawn, ladder, Shell and StdioProcess tests pass unchanged, and after full Marrow.Core.Tests and Marrow.Services.Tests runs no helper is left on the machine. Not changed: ShellTests' "killed exactly one second later" test needs the PowerShell helper to deliver within 500 ms of real time, and fails under parallel load before and after this decision alike (6 and 8 of 8 runs at four suites in parallel; passes alone).

## ED-246

[UI][SCROLL][FRAMES] One soft, weighted scrolling behaviour for every scroll area (OD-0071; OD-0069; OD-0076; frames per ED-237). AMENDED 2026-10-02 after the review of 975fcae2a refuted its first version on ten points (the superseded behaviour is in that commit). Before ED-246: every ScrollViewer was stock Avalonia (a notch jumped 50 points, Page Up/Down a page, a touch flick stopped dead, a touchpad's fractions each jumped, the terminal scrolled a line per touchpad event; audit E:/Droppy/work/review-scroll-physics/port-today.md). Measured Mac physics: E:/Droppy/work/review-scroll-physics/mac-physics.md (both reference videos are wheel-mouse only). DECISION, src/Marrow.UI/Port/SoftScroll.cs: (1) Reach: `SoftScroll.Install()` (PortControlThemes.Register) puts class handlers on the ScrollViewer type, so every ScrollViewer gets the behaviour whatever its template. (2) One model: every input is a distance delivered over time (a report spread evenly over the interval since the previous report of its stream, a stream's first over 8 ms, reports more than 34 ms apart starting a new burst) and the view follows that path through one first-order lag, solved exactly between breakpoints (a spread ending, braking onto an end, arriving), so 60 and 240 Hz sample the same curve. (3) Input is classified from the stream (WheelClassifier; Avalonia passes WM_MOUSEWHEEL's WHEEL_DELTA units / 120 and nothing else): a stream whose reports are all multiples of 120 is a notched wheel; one whose greatest common divisor divides 120 and is at least 8 is a high-resolution or free-spinning wheel (Logitech: 15); anything else is a precision touchpad, and a touchpad stream stays one to its end (streams split at a 0.1 s gap). Both wheels take the wheel's lag, 0.071 s, the Mac's measured flick decay (section 4: tau 0.071 s); a touchpad takes a 4 ms lag. A stream that turns out to be a touchpad's switches lag with position and speed continuous. A high-resolution wheel's 8 x 15 units travel exactly 50 points and its speed falls with tau 0.0710 s after its last report (975fcae2a gave it the 0.5 s touchpad coast). (4) Weight and start: the view moves in the first frame after a notch (0.75 points of 50 at 240 Hz, 8.2 at 60 Hz; 975fcae2a: 0.48) and a flick's speed is highest as its last report's interval ends (5 notches in 50 ms: peak at 60 ms, distance / peak 0.110 s; 8 notches: 56 ms, 0.105 s; 20 notches: 52 ms, 0.102 s; the Mac's 0.0998 s; fitted decay 0.0710 s; 975fcae2a: 64 ms and 0.117 s, 60 ms and 0.115 s, 60 ms and 0.113 s). Against the Mac's recorded flicks, with the input assumed as notches spread over 50 ms (port-vs-mac-wheel-flicks.png), the port's peak speed is 0.99, 0.65, 0.98, 1.16, 1.25 and 0.64 of the Mac's (chat C1, picker P1 and P2, diff D1, theme list T1 and T4; 975fcae2a: 0.89, 0.59, 0.89, 1.05, 1.17, 0.59), reached 52-60 ms after the burst starts (975fcae2a: 60-65 ms); the low ones are flicks whose Mac input was shorter than the assumed 50 ms, which the videos cannot settle. (5) The touchpad: the port adds no coast of its own to a touchpad stream. ENGINEERING DECISION: Windows' precision-touchpad stack continues a legacy WM_MOUSEWHEEL stream with its own decaying inertial deltas after a lift, and fingers resting on the pad send nothing, so the stream itself says when the motion stops; a coast on top would stack two tails, and a coast planned at every pause coasts a hold. UNVERIFIED: no touchpad gesture could be recorded from this session (this PC has a precision-touchpad collection on its Logitech receiver, and a gesture needs a hand). The probe E:/Droppy/work/review-scroll-physics/probe/WheelProbe.cs (a plain Win32 window as Avalonia makes, logging WM_MOUSEWHEEL / WM_MOUSEHWHEEL with message time, QPC time, delta, extra info and the raw-input device; self-test probe/selftest.csv) records it; if a lift turns out to end the stream with no tail, a coast is to be added back on the stream's shape. A steady stroke (4 points every 8 ms) runs 0.79, 1.63, 1.92, 2.03, 2.06, 2.08 points and then 2.083 every frame at 240 Hz, 6.36 then 8.333 at 60 Hz (975fcae2a: 1.62, 1.14, 3.04, 2.54, then a 2.2 / 2.0 alternation); a stroke that moves then holds rests where the fingers stopped, 33 ms after its last report; a flick followed by a decaying tail rests on the stream's own sum 25 ms after its last report (port-vs-mac-touchpad.png). A touchpad stream stays with the scroll view it started on (latching, as macOS latches a gesture). (6) Touch (touch screens and pens through Avalonia's presenter): the drag is the presenter's; the release coasts with UIKit's normal deceleration rate, 0.998 per ms (tau 0.4995 s; UNVERIFIED, parked: no trackpad in the reference videos; re-measure with the clip requested in mac-physics.md section 7) and travels exactly v tau (500 points a second: 249.75 points, where 975fcae2a stopped about 5 points short at 10 points a second). (7) Every motion ends exactly: the lag aims 2 points a second's worth past its stop and rests the moment it arrives, so the last step is the smallest (one notch at 240 Hz ends 0.0096, 0.0091, 0.0081 points; 975fcae2a: 0.0128 then a 0.2115 settle). A spring curve, which never quite arrives (`.smooth(0.25)` is 0.8 % short at its settling duration; 975fcae2a snapped 8.6 points of 1000 there, 8.1 for `.smooth(0.35)`), is run on and scaled by 1 + 0.05 points / distance so it arrives exactly with its last step a sliver (at most 0.05 points from the Swift curve); a speed carried into an animation is carry t (1 - t/T)^2 e^(-t/fade), exactly nothing, with no speed, at the end T (975fcae2a: about 1.7 points left at a carried 20 000 points a second). (8) The ends: no overscroll and no spring-back (every Mac case measured, section 6). DEPARTURE from the Mac under OD-0071 (soft, weighted): where the Mac stops from speed in one frame (last-frame speed 0.19-0.88 of the peak), the port keeps its speed until it is within 12 ms of the end at that speed and then brakes onto it with the speed continuous (a 12 ms lag, or the motion's own lag if shorter): 8 notches into the theme list's 276-point end are still at 0.31 of their peak speed 10 points out and rest 75 ms later; from half the peak speed to rest takes 83 ms (975fcae2a: 0.05 of the peak 10 points out, 279 ms, and 442 ms: an ease). A touch coast lands the same way; a touchpad stream follows its own clamped path with its 4 ms lag. Reports toward an end keep going to a view still moving that way, so a flick into an end keeps its notches and lands with their speed. (9) Wheel chaining: a scroll view takes a report when its target can still move that way or it is moving that way; one at rest at its end hands the report on to the scroll view around it, as Avalonia's presenter does (handled only when the offset changes, ScrollViewer.IsScrollChainingEnabled); with chaining off it keeps it (975fcae2a swallowed the wheel at the end of the Settings multi-line editor and of the MCP form's arguments editor). (10) Keys: Page Up/Down page by the viewport and Home/End go to the ends along `.smooth(duration: 0.25)` (ENGINEERING DECISION: the source's own short programmatic curve, DiffInspector.swift:104), only for a key the focused control and everything between it and the scroll view left unhandled (a bubbling class handler after each element's own handling; 975fcae2a took them in the tunnelling phase from sliders and list items). A scroll view in a control's template (a list's, a text box's) waits for that control first; Avalonia's own ScrollViewer.OnKeyDown jump and TextBox's ScrollViewer.PageDown jump are taken back and glide instead. Sliders keep Home, End and the page keys (BackdropOpacitySlider, the wallpaper softness slider), a list item's keys are its list's, a text field's are its own (Avalonia's TextBox takes Page Up/Down too). (11) Programmatic: `SoftScroll.ScrollTo(viewer, offset, animation)` replays the caller's SwiftUI curve (ThreadTimeline .smooth(0.35) jump, .easeOut(0.25) send; SidebarView the transaction's; DiffInspector .smooth(0.25) as Swift :104) and carries in any running speed; the reader's input takes over from it (a report against it starts from where the view is). An instant ScrollTo, or an offset another piece of code sets (anchoring, BringIntoView), moves a running motion along with it. (12) Phases: SwiftUI's ScrollPhase (interacting while a touchpad stream or a touch drag runs, decelerating in a touch coast, animating for a programmatic scroll; a wheel reports none, ThreadTimeline.swift:466-467). (13) The indicator follows the Mac: shown only on an axis whose visibility is Auto or Visible (`.scrollIndicators(.automatic)`, the Swift default and Popovers.swift:111), never on Hidden (`.never` / showsIndicators: false: ThreadTimeline.swift:436, SettingsView.swift:190 and :229, SidebarView.swift:139, RootView.swift:347, ProjectIconPicker.swift:155, the horizontal strips). It is drawn as Windows 11's own overlay scroll bar and follows Windows' "Always show scrollbars" (HKCU Control Panel\Accessibility DynamicScrollbars = 0), as the Mac's scroller follows macOS's "Show scroll bars": off (the default), a 2-point line appears while the view scrolls or the pointer moves over it and fades out 2 s after the last of either (0.1 s in, 0.5 s out), widening to a 6-point thumb in a 12-point bar with its track and arrows once the pointer has rested on the bar 0.4 s (over 0.1 s) and narrowing 2 s after it leaves; on, the full bar stays. The full bar is a scroll bar (the thumb drags, a track click pages, the arrows step); the thin line lets the pointer through. ComposerTextView's view keeps overlay scrollers whatever the setting (ComposerTextView.swift:236-238 scrollerStyle = .overlay, autohidesScrollers). SOURCE FACT for the timings: WinUI 2.8's ScrollBar resources on this PC (Microsoft.UI.Xaml 2.8 resources.pri: 0.40 s expand begin, 2.00 s contract begin, 0.1 s expand; the key-to-value pairing read from their order). UNVERIFIED: the 2/6/12-point sizes, the thumb colour (black 0.447 / white 0.545, ControlStrongFillColorDefault as recalled), the track colour and the 0.5 s fade. 975fcae2a's invented 6-point knob with its 1.45 s fade is gone. (14) The terminal (not a ScrollViewer): TerminalSurface drives its history with the same ScrollDriver in points, with a row quantum: a notch is one row (SwiftTerm MacTerminalView.swift:3232-3236) and glides there; a touchpad's or a fine wheel's fractions follow in fractions of a row, and a stream that stops between rows runs on, forward, from the speed it has onto the next whole row (its lag stretched to keep that speed, at most 0.25 s), never back and never a stop then a creep (975fcae2a glided from rest toward the nearest row, backwards about half the time). Page keys glide; typing returns to the live screen at once. (15) Reduce motion: every input steps at once. (16) Frames: FrameClock.Source (ED-237), one request per motion, none at rest; per frame a few exponentials per axis and one Offset write. Also: SidebarView's list presenter and the MCP form's presenter are transparent (a notch inside a row freeze or over a gap reached nothing). Evidence: SoftScrollTests and SoftScrollReviewTests (Marrow.UI.Tests, per-frame at 60 and 240 Hz with reports at their own times between frames: the notch against its closed form, 60 = 240 Hz, a flick's peak and decay, continuity across notches and a lag switch, reversal, classification, a fine wheel's glide with no coast, move-then-hold, Windows' tail not stacked, the first 150 ms of a steady stroke, every motion's last step, the ends, the touch coast's exact distance, programmatic curves and carry-in run to their ends, rows, keys on sliders, lists and text fields, chaining, the Windows 11 indicator, Always show, overlay-only), SoftScrollCoverageTests and SoftScrollAppInputTests (Marrow.App.Tests: every scroll template glides, the terminal's notch, touchpad rows at 60 and 240 Hz and page keys, the Settings sliders, the MCP arguments editor's chaining).
